CAPT.     WALTER NORTON was son of Thomas and Alice (Cran-
mer)   Norton of  the  manor  of  Sharpenhoe  in  Bedfordshire.         His
father was famous as the author of Gorboduc, and married into the
Cranmer family (his first wife being a daughter of Archbishop Thomas
Cranmer,    and his second wife,   the mother of our subject,    being a
daughter of the Archbishop's brother.)     Walter Norton was a soldier
of fortune,   and early became associated with Sir Ferdinando Gorges
in his work in New England.       He was probably among the members
of the Gorges  Company which arrived at Wessagussett about  the
middle of September,   1623.   He was here before Winthrop arrived,
andwas selected with others to hold an inquest at Charlestown be
 - 456 - 
446                                             OLIVER
foreGovernor Winthrop and Isaac Johnson,  Esq., on 18 Sept. 1630.
He desired to be made afreeman of Massachusetts Bay Colony,   19
Oct. 1630,   andwas madea freeman,   18 May,  1631.    (Register,  3:  90.)
The Council for New England granted 100 acres in Maine to him,
Samuel Maverick, William Jefferyes andJohn Bursley,  for each per-
son that they would transport to New England within seven years,
2 Dec.  1631.    In the Council records these men were described as
"of  New England."    (Records  of the  Council  for  New  England,
AmericanAntiquarian Society Proceedings,   1867,   p.    101.)    He was
living at Agamenticus (York) in 1632,  and sailed from thence with
Capt.  John Stone and John Oldham and three others.          In the course
of their voyage they werebarbarously murderedby the Indians near
the Connecticut River.      Governor Winthrop tells of this  event on
21  Jan.   1633-34,    and adds  that  Capt.     Stone took  Capt.     Norton
aboard  at Agamenticus.        He married  (1)   in  England,   Mrs.  Jane
(Reve) Reynolds,  the mother ofhis children.        He married (2) Eleanor
-,who survived him and married (2) William Hooke, an earlyGov-
ernor of the Province of Maine.       William was the son of Humphrey
Hooke,    alderman of the city of Bristol,   Eng.,  and was at York as
early as 1633.    Hewas styled"citizen and merchant of Bristol,  Eng-
land now of Agamenticus" when he purchased one-third of a patent
whichhadbeengranted to Humphrey Hooke in 1637.    This was in
1638.    He was one of the attorneys for Gorges in 1641,  and removed
to Salisbury in 1643.    The inventory of his estate was taken 11 Apr.
1654.
Mrs.  Eleanor  Hooke,  late wife of Mr. William Hooke,   deceased,
petitioned to theGeneral Court concerning his estate,  29 May,  1655.
Onthe same day she petitioned"to make sale of lands at Accomen-
ticus,    now Yorke,   that  have been formerly  appropriated to Capt.
[Walter]  Norton,  heretofore hir husband," and the Court granted her
power so  to  do.         (Massachusetts  Bay Colony  Records,   4:   Pt.     1,
234,  235.)     She was plaintiff  in a suit against Mr. John Alcocke,   16
Oct. 1660.    She was living in Boston near 1667.
Childrenbywife Jane, born in England:
Thomas,     d.    in 1627.
Jane,     m.     (1)  Henry Simpson of York,    Me.,  and m.    (2)  Nicholas
Bond of York and Portsmouth,   N. H.
OLIVER
JONATHAN  OLIVER resided in the South Parish of Weymouth,
1777  to  1782.     He was not listed as head of any family living  in
Massachusetts in 1790.    A Jonathan Oliver,   whose family consisted
of one maleover 16 years,   four males under 16 and three females,  was
living  in Nobleborough,     Me. ,     in   1790.    (Maine  Census,      35.)     No
other state shows any Jonathan Oliver in 1790.

tion of marriage  in Boston,     13  May,    1774.    Their  intention was

PARKER
REV.    JAMES  PARKER appears to have come to New England
before 3 July,   1632.    (Records  of  the  Court  of Assistants,     2:   25.)
Hewas granted four acres of land in Dorchester,  5Mar. 1633.    (Dor-
chester Town Records,  Register,   21:  167.)     His lands  there were re-
ferred to 29 Dec. 1634.    He was made a freeman of the Massachusetts
Bay  Colony,       14 May,    1634  (Register,    3:92.)     He  married,     near
1635,        Mary  Maverick,     daughter  of  Rev.  John  and  Mary  (Gye)
Maverick,   who came to Massachusetts in the Maryand John,   arriving
at Nantasket,  30 May,  1630.    She undoubtedly came to Dorchester
with her parents.
Mr.  Parker soon appears among the Weymouth settlers.     He was
appointed   " to  end  small  causes"   in  Weymouth,      9  June,       1639.
(Massachusetts Bay Colony Records,  1:  263.)     He was also chosen
adeputy from Weymouth to  the General  Court,    1639,     1640  and
 - 467 - 
PARKMAN                               457
1641.    The General Court allowed him to "sell  strong water"  at
Weymouth,   2 June,   1641.    He was authorized "to see people joyne
in marriage &keepe record  thereof"  for  Weymouth,   and,    28 Jan.
1640-41,   the General Court entered the following upon its  records:
"Mr.  James Parker is  alowed to marry Thomas Clifton and Mary
Butterworth  within  a month."    He was  appointed "clerk  of  the
writs"  for  Weymouth,   10 Dec.  1641.    He again served as Deputy
in 1642 and 1643.   He was present at the session of the General
Court held in Boston,   10 May,   1643.    (Massachusetts Bay Colony
Records,    2:   23,    33.)
Writing in that  year Governor John Winthrop said:     " Those of
the  lower  part  of the river  Pascataquack  invited  one  Mr.  James
Parker of Weymouth,   agodly man and a scholar,  one who had been
many years a deputy for  the public court,  to be their  minister. "
(Winthrop History,   2:93.)    Winthrop  also  gives  a list  of "Gifts
bestowed upon the colony since 1634," among which was the follow-
ing:    " Mr.  Parker  of  Weymouth,  his  brother,     £300,       £50 to  Mr.
Parker and Mr. Stone their disposing. "    ( Ibid.      2 :    342.)
From Portsmouth,   N. H.,   he removed to Barbados shortly before
24 June,    1646.    Here he spent the remainder of his life.         He made
his will  21 Aug. 1648,   and it was entered for probate 26 Aug.  1652.
Hementions his son John Parker,   his wife Mary Parker and his chil-
drenAzricam,  James,  Thomas,   Fearnot and Mary Parker.          His wife
to be executrix.            Mr.  Richard  Gregory  and  Mr.  Richard  Vines
executors  in  Barbados,     and his  brothers  Mr.  Elias  Maverick and
Mr.  Moses  Maverick  executors  in  New England.        (Register,    68:
202.)    Fearnot Parker married in the parish of St.  John,    Barbados,
19 Mar.  1660-61,    Capt.   John Parnell.      James Parker,   the son,   died
inBoston in 1660.
Rev.  James  Parker's  brother  John Parker,   haberdasher,    died  in
the parish of St. Pancras,  Soper Lane,  London, between 14 May and
27 Aug.  1639,    and his brother Joseph Parker,   skinner,    of the same
parish,    died  there  between  15  Oct.  1642,    and 3 Dec.  1644.    The
latter in his will mentioned his "brother James Parker in New Eng-
land and his  children. "    Joseph Parker was a native of Leicester,
Eng.         (Register,   46:   308-310. )

CAPT.      WILLIAM   PERKINS,   the  first  schoolmaster  of which
there is any record, was voted £10 for six months'   schooling,    10 Mar.
1651.     (Weymouth Town Records.)    He entered Emmanuel College,
Cambridge,     as a pensioner at  Michaelmas Term,    1625;      afterwards
immigrated to  Christ's  College from which he graduated,    A.B.,     at
lent term,   1627-28.
He was son of William Perkins,   a merchant tailor,  of London,  and
was born 25 Aug.  1607,   and came in the ship William and Francis,
leaving  London,    7 Mar.  1631-32.             This  ship  arrived at Boston,     5
June,    1632.    (Drake's,   The Founders of New England,   11.)    He was
madea freeman of the Massachusetts Bay Colony, 3Sept.  1634.   He
married at Roxbury,   30 Aug. 1636,   Elizabeth Wootton,   and removed
to Weymouth in 1643,  where he resided till  1652,  when he removed
toGloucester,    and in 1655 to Topsfield.         He became the first minister
of the latter  place.      He was deputy from Weymouth in 1644 and
Captain there in 1645.    He died at Topsfield,   21  May,      1682,    aged
75 years.
The General Court entered the following record on 7 Oct.  1641 :
"Mr: Willi Perkins,   for his fathers £50,   is granted 400 acres of land. "
(Massachusetts  Bay Colony Records,    1: 338.)     He was to  "have
power to end small causes at Waymoth, "  29 May,    1644,    and again,
14 May,    1645.    (Ibid.      2:    73,   97.)    He was a deputy at the General
Court,     29 May,    1644,    and was called " Lieut.   Wm.   Perkins "   (Ibid.
66)  and " Capt., "  4 Nov.  1646.    ( Ibid.      184.)
The English ancestry of the above William Perkins  is  published
in  the  New England Historical  and Genealogical  Register   (1922) ,
Volume 74,    pages 223-232.

PETTEE
This surname is  also found spelled  Pattee,   Pettee,  Pettes,   Pettis,

1.  WILLIAM  PETTEE settled  in Weymouth near  1638;     died
there between 14 Apr. and 24 June,   1679.    The town granted him
ten acres "in Ester neck, "  three acres "lyinge neare the mill" and
five acres "at london Berge."    He received lot No. 24 in the great
lots,   26 Nov.  1651,   and twelve acres in the First Division and thirty-
six in the Second Division,  14 Dec. 1663.    (Weymouth Land Grants,
259,   281,     282,    283.)   His wife was Mary     , who survived her hus-
band.       He was a selectman in 1643,   1666 and perhaps other years.
Inhis will he bequeathed to his wife Mary,  to his eldest son Joseph,
to his sons Samuel and William and to his daughter Mary,    the wife
ofHenry Adams.       Witnesses:   Jonas Humphrey andWilliam Chard.
His inventory was appraised 24 June,  1679,  by William Torrey and
JonasHumphrey;   sworn to by his son Joseph and his widow Mary,
29 July,   1679.    (Morse's Genealogical Register, 2:  148.)   Hedeposed
calling himself about 72 years of age,  30 July,  1667.    (Suffolk Court
Files,   815,    paper 38.)   Hencehe was born near 1595.

PHILLIPS
1.   DEACON  NICHOLAS  PHILLIPS first  appears in New Eng-
landas an inhabitant of Dedhamwith HenryPhillips,  Martin Phillips,
Abraham Shaw and over 120 others.        He was an inhabitant of Con-
tentment (Dedham)  before 18 Aug.  1636 (Dedham Town Records,
1: 20),   and on that dayhad twelve acres granted to him there.       He
laid "downe a p'cell  of ground for aburiall place"  at  Dedham,      6
Apr.  1638.    He was chosen "to mowe," gather up and bring home
thatch  for  y Meeting  house,"  28 Aug.  1638.    He purchased a lot
of Philemon Dalton and sold the same to  Henry Phillips  before  1
Mar.  1641.    (Dedham Town Records,  1:  84.)    He is last mentioned
on the Town Records  of  Dedham,   under date 23 Feb. 1650  (page
178).               He was made a freeman  of the  Massachusetts  Bay Colony,
13 May,   1640.    (Register 3: 187.)
"Deacon  Phillips"  received  thirteen  acres  in  the  First  Division
and thirty-nine acres in the Second Division in Weymouth,   14 Dec.
1663.    (Weymouth Land Grants,   282,   283.)    His lands were adjoining
the lands ofMartin Phillips (Ibid.   272).     Hewas one of the appraisers
ofthe estate of William Brandon ofWeymouth,  23 Nov. 1646 (Regis-
ter,     7 :         35),       and of  Dorothy King's estate,    18 Oct.  1652.    He was
called Deacon Phillips,  8 Feb.  1660.

PITTS
ELIZABETH  PITTS of Dorchester signed a receipt 21 Nov. 1639.
(Records and Files  of  Quarterly  Courts  of Essex  County,      1:   12.)
She,    or another person of the same name,   was admitted to the First
Church of Charlestown 13 Aрг.     1643.
Administration on the estate of Mrs. Elizabeth Pitts,  deceased at
Weymouth, was granted to William Holbrook and Elizabeth,  his wife,
1 Aug. 1655.    The inventory was taken by JohnWhitmarsh,   Thomas
Bayley,   Samuel Parker and James Nash,   total,    £16 6s.    6d.             Their
account reads:    "My Mother Mrs. Pitts oweth to me for attendance
in her sickness of 26weeks,   £10. "     (Suffolk Probate, 3:  26.)
Therefore Elizabeth,   the wife of William Holbrook of Weymouth,
1655,   was a daughter of Elizabeth Pitts.        The daughter may or may
not have been born a Pitts.

POOLE
1.   CAPT.    EDWARD  POOLE,  aged 26,    servant to George Allen,
came in Rev.  Joseph  Hull's  Company,   sailing  from Weymouth,    in
Dorset,   on or near 20 Mar.  1634-35.          He was granted five acres on
"the  plaine  the streete"  and two acres "at  the steping  stone  the
swampe.   "     He was granted one of the great lots on the east side of
Fresh  Pond,     2 Feb.  1651-52.        He also  had six  acres  in the First
Division and eighteen acres in the Second Division granted to him,
14 Dec.  1663.    (Weymouth Land Grants,     257,     281,    282,     283.)
He married,       between  1641  and  1645,     Sarah  Pinney  (Pynney) ,
niece of Humphrey Pinney of Dorchester,   and daughter of John and
Protesia (Holdich)  Pinney of Exeter,   Eng.         (Edward Poole MSS.   ,      in
New England  Historic  Genealogical  Society,     Boston. )
Edward Poole  of Weymouth,   sawyer,   gave power of attorney to
William Pardon to receive a legacy given unto Sarah,   wife  of said
Edwardby the last will of Edmund Pinney of Broadway,    Somerset-
shire,      and also another legacy given to Sarah by Elizabeth Stander-
wick of Broadway,  5 Dec.  1645.    (Aspinwall Notarial Records,    12.)
Her  father's  will,     made  25  May,      1637,      and  her  uncle   Edmund
Pinney's  will  are  published  in  the New  England  Historical   and
Genealogical Register,  63:  36-42.
He died at Weymouth between 22 Aug. and 16 Sept.  1664,     and
his  widow deposed  26  Oct.  1664.     Edward  Poole  of  Weymouth,
"being sicke," made his will 22Aug. 1664.  Unto his wife (not named)
he gave his dwelling and land adjoining so " long as she doth keepe
her selfe a widow" and two acres purchased of John Prince and then
to his son Samuel.            His son Isaac to have the lot of 18 acres that was
Weavers.               To his son Joseph  his great lot  and one-half  of the lot

"John Long of Weymouth in New England,   husbandman aged
about twenty foure yeares sworne saith upon his oath that whereas
Mary Lane was to serve Richard Silvester  of Weymouth aforesaid
for the space offoure yeares or thereabouts from about the beginning
ofthe first month last  (Mar. 1640-41]   as this deponent hath credibly
heard,    one Edward Pole of Weymouth in the first  moneth aforesaid
was Deserous to marry her &to buy out her time of service aforesaid
and in this  deponents  hearing  did promise  to  pay unto the  said
Richard Silvester for the same two hundred foot of boards and foure
pounds in money or such good commodities as he should like ofupon
Midsomer eve next & then the said Pole was to take her away &
marry her.   "      (Lechford's Note-Book,   1638-41,    p.      391.)

Edward Bates,   aged 63 years or thereabouts,    and Mary Raines,
aged about 28 years,   say that being present with Samuel Poole of
Weymouth when he lay upon his death bed he did declare that his
wife should have all his estate until his daughter Mary come of age
or was married.        Secondly  that  at age or marriage his  daughter
should have half of his estate and at the death of her mother the
whole.       In case she die before age or marriage his wife should pay
his  brother  Benjamin  Poole  £3.            Elder  Edward Bates  and Mary
Raines made oath at a County Court held in Boston 30 Apr.  1669.

1.   RICHARD  PORTER,  husbandman, came in Rev. Joseph Hull's
Company,   sailing  from Weymouth in Dorset,  on or near  20 Mar.
1634-35.                He was one of the twenty-one families  "to sit  down at
Wessaguscus, "  8 July,  1635.   He was made a freeman of the Massa-
chusetts  Bay Colony,  18  May,    1653.    (Register,    3:    192. )     He died
atWeymouth between 25 Dec. 1688,  and 6 Mar. 1688-89.           He made
his will at Weymouth,   25 Dec. 1688,   and the inventory of his estate
was taken 6 Mar.  1688-89.          To his grandchild Thomas Porter,   only
 - 496 - 
486                                       PORTER
son of his son Thomas Porter,  deceased,  he gave his dwelling house,
barn,   orchard and land adjoining,  and other lands at 21 years.            If
said grandchild die before 21 the estate to go to his grandchild Ruth
Richards on conditions,   or to his son John.     To his grandchild Samuel
Bayley two acres onKing Oak Hill.        To his daughter Mary Bicknell
£10.         Remainder  of  estate  to his  son John  Porter.        His  friends
James Lovell,   Sr.,   and Thomas Reed,  overseers.         Witnesses:    Abiah
Whitman,       Zachariah   Bicknell   and  Stephen  French,     Sr.      (Porter
Genealogy,   8,   9.)
He was granted one of the great  lots "on the east side of Fresh
Pond" 2 Feb. 1651-52,   and ten acres in the First Division and thirty
acres  in  the  Second  Division,     14  Dec.  1663.     (Weymouth  Land

14.  THOMAS  PORTER  (Thomas,       Sergt.    John²)  was born  at

He married at Weymouth,   24 Jan.  1739-40,   Mercy Bates,   daughter

Bates,   as above indicated.
Thomas Porter,   the younger,   died at Weymouth shortly before 31
Mar.  1759,     without having settled his father's estate.       Administra-
tion was granted to his widow,  13 Apr. 1759.   Ezra Whitmarsh,    Jacob
Goold,    John  Porter,    Jr. ,       Matthew Pratt  and Ebenezer  Pratt  were
appointed to make a division  of the estate.        They first  set off  to
Susannah Porter,  widow of Thomas Porter,  late of Weymouth,    her
thirds.      They then set off to MercyPorter her thirds of the real estate
of Thomas Porter,   " ye younger,"  late  of Weymouth,   and  assigned
her one-third of the dwelling she now lives  in,    and to  the  widow
Susannah  Porter they assigned the remaining part of the dwelling,
6 Mar. 1760.    (Suffolk Probate,   54:    283,  289;     56:   286. )     They resided
in the North Parish.

Ebenezer Porter of Weymouth,  gentleman, "laboring under many
bodily infirmities," made his will 11 Jan. 1763,   and it was proved 7
Oct.  1763.    To his wife Tabitha he gave the use of his whole estate
until his youngest son arrives at 21.    To his daughter Ruth Tirrell
£4,    she already having had a portion.          To his  daughter  Jael  £13
6s.    8d.         To his daughters Tabitha and Mary like sums.      To his sons
Ebenezer and Ezekiel the remainder equally to be divided when his
youngest  son arrives  at  21.    Wife,    executrix.         Witnesses:    James
Humphrey,      Samuel  Pratt   "y" 3d,"  and Ezra  Porter.      Inventory,
£453 10s.    4d.              (Suffolk Probate,   62:   453.)

PRATT
PHINEHAS  PRATT,  one of the earliest Englishmen to inhabit at
Wessagusset and one of the first to forsake the place, came with nine
others  in  the  Sparrow  in  May,     1622,     to  find  a suitable  place  for
Thomas Weston's Company.        They selected a place called by the
Indians Wessagusset or Wessaguscus.          They were joined by Weston's
Company of about sixty persons in July,   1622.
This "old planter" Pratt fled fromWessagusset to Plymouth over-
land in the winter following,   arriving  there 24 Mar.  1622-23.             He
remained at Plymouth for several years,   and there married in  1630
MaryGodbertson,  a daughter of Godbert Godbertson (Cuthbertson),
who came from  Leyden to  Plymouth  in  1623.   He removed  from
Plymouth to Charlestown  in 1648,   and ever  afterwards lived there.
He died at  Charlestown,   19 Apr.  1680,    aged  "about 90 yrs.  "    He
made his  will  8 Jan.  1677,   and his  inventory was taken 21 May,
1680.    In his  will he styled  himself a "joiner  being  very  aged. "
He mentions his  wife Mary,  his son Joseph Pratt and the "rest of
my children. "
1.   MATTHEW¹ PRATT,  whose Christian name appears as Macute,
Macuth,    Macaeth,   Micareth,   was "an old resident"  of Weymouth.
He had twenty acres granted to him " in the mill field"  (now East
Weymouth)   and eighteen  acres  on the west  side  of " mill  River.  "
Hewas made a freeman of the Massachusetts Bay Colony 13 May,
1640.    In Feb.  1648,  he was chosen a"townsman"  (selectman).        He
died at Weymouth,  29 Aug. 1672.   He made his  will 25 Mar.  1672,
and it  was proved 30 Apr. 1673.    To his wife Elizabeth Pratt the use
of his estate for her natural life.            To son Thomas Pratt lands after
his wife's decease,   and land at " Hollie" upon condition that he pay
"my Daughter Chard"  £4.         To son Matthew Pratt lands on like
condition.              To son John Pratt " an ewe and lamb. "   To son Samuel
Pratt land near his house.         To son Joseph Pratt a lot at the pond.
To his daughter Chard £7,   and to her daughter Johannah Chard his
best  bed.            To his  daughter  White  a parcel  of  land.          To his  son
Thomas Pratt's daughter Sarah £5.           To Thomas Pratt's son William
Pratt half of a mare.        Wife to be executrix.          " His Pastor Mr. Samuel
Torrey and his Kinsman Elder Edward Bates,  and his son Thomas
Pratt"  to  be  overseers.                  Witnesses:            Edward  Bates  and  Thomas
Dyer.           The  inventory  of  Mathew  Pratt  who  deceased  Aug.  29,
1672,     was taken 12 Dec.  1672.    (Pratt Genealogy,    1889,   pp.      19-21. )

bounds.  "    This  lot  was apparently  a little  southeast  from Lincoln
Square.           Ephraim  Pratt  of  Weymouth,     yeoman,    " being  sick  of
body" made his will 25 Apr. 1749,  and it was probated 3 Nov. 1769,
twenty years later.        To his wife Lydia Pratt he gave one-half of his
estate and the other half to  " his  cousin Ephraim Pratt son of his
Brother "  at  the age of 21 years.         If he die before he is  of age,    his
brother Joseph Pratt shall  have his part.       To his cousin Zachariah
Shaw he gave Shaws cedar swamp.             To his cousin Deborah Butt a
bed and bolster.         His  brother  John  Burrell  to  be executor.          The
latter reonunced this trust 5 Nov.  1769,   and Ephraim Pratt was ap-
pointed  administrator.          The widow's  thirds  were set  off  to her  11
Jan.  1770.    (Suffolk  Probate,    68:     347,   482.)    He had no issue,    and
the Pratt Genealogy is in error on page 211 .

PRIEST
JAMES  PRIEST was to  have allotments of land "at Mannings
Moone"  in Dorchester,    2 Jan.  1637.    (Dorchester  Town Records,
29.)     On 3 Apr.  1638,   "it  is ordered that the allotment which was
formerly graunted  on Mannings  Moone shall  be 8 ake  to  James
Priest"   (Ibid.       32.)     On 14 Mar. 1652-53,   "It is voted that whereas
Walter Harris desireth a little p'cell of land,  p'cell of the garden be-
longing to Priestes howse, and which he form'ly have enjoyed,  to by
the same,    it is by vote left  unto the selectmen."    (Ibid.     315.)    He
was made a freeman of the  Massachusetts  Bay Colony,     10 May,
1643.    Heremoved to Weymouth,   near 1639,  and spent the rest of his
life there.         He had lands granted to him at Weymouth " in King Oke
hill" and "in the east  ffield,"  (Weymouth Land Grants,   272.)    He
also had five acres in the First Division and fifteen acres in the Sec-
ond Division granted,  14 Dec. 1663.
James Priest,     may have been the James Priest,   son of Abraham
and Elizabeth (Nuens)  Priest,  who was baptized at Chesham,   county
of Bucks,     5 Nov.  1610.    (Register,  65:   66.)
James Priest,    "being sicke and weake of body," made his  will  at
Boston,    4 Mar.  1675-76,  and it was probated 28 Apr. 1676.    To his
son "Sedrach Thare"  his lot of 27 acres in Weymouth woods.           To
his wife his "housing, land and cattle at Weymouth and what right I
have in a house at Boston that I now live in."    Wife to be executrix.
"His son-in-law Sedreck Thare and Decon Thomas Dyar of Way-
mouth"   overseers.       Witnesses:  "Edward  Sale  and  John  Dyar."
(Suffolk Probate 6:  117.)     Inventory of the estate ofJames Priest of
Weymouth,   late deceased apprised,   11 Apr. 1676,  by Samuel White
and Ebenezer  White.       Items:  house and land at Weymouth £44:

RANDALL                                 559
RANDALL
1.   ROBERT  RANDALL came from Wendover,  county of Bucks,
England,     to  Weymouth before 1640.    He was born near 1608 and
diedatWeymouth, 3 May,  1691.   He deposed 2 July,  1688,  that he
was "aged Eighty yeares or thereabouts, " andthat he was living for
some time in Wendover in the county of Bucks within the Realm of
England,    ... anddid well know Enoch Hunt of Titenden in the parish
of Lee about two miles distant from Wendover," etc.    (Massachusetts
State Archives,     129:    16.)     The parish registers  of Wendover begin
in 1632,    and a careful search of them revealed no trace of any person
of the name Randall.       He married (1)  Mary      ,  who was buried
at  Weymouth,    3 Sept.  1640.    He married  (2)  Mary French,     sister
of Stephen French,  who calls her "my sister  Mary Randall"  in his
will  in  1679.    He was admitted afreeman of the Massachusetts Bay
Colony,    26 May,    1647.    He had three lots granted to him " in  the
East field, "  and seven acres  in the First  Division,   and twenty-one
acres   in  the   Second  Division,     the  latter  granted  14  Dec.  1663.
(Weymouth Land Grants,  258,    283.)
Robert Randall of Weymouth, "being weake of body,"  made his
will 27 Mar. 1691,   and it was probated 25 May,   1691.    Τo his eldest
son John he gave several lots,  one "in the Range Field," another in
the First Division.         To his youngest son Thomashe gave his dwelling
house,    etc.     To his  daughters  Mary,   wife  of Abraham Staples  of
Mendon,      and Hannah,    wife of John Warfield  of  Mendon,    to each
£5.                 Son John to  be  executor.           Witnesses:      Mary Vining,      Joseph
Dyer and William Chard.        Inventory taken 16 May,  1691 ,     by John
Shaw and Joseph Dyer.         (Suffolk Probate,    8:    41,   42.)

READE
WILLIAM  READE was  elected  a " Townsman"  (selectman)  at
Weymouth,       26  Nov.  1651.     (Weymouth Town Records. )    As such
anoffice could then be held only by those who had taken the free-
man's oath,    it  is  conjectured that the first  William Reade who re-
moved  to  Boston  returned  to  Weymouth for  a short  period,      and
while living in the ancient town was elected a "Townsman. "

REDDING
JOHN REDDING,   a seaman,  aresident in Weymouth,  sells land
in Cascoe Bay unto Edward Budd of Boston,   carver,   upon the west
side of " Henry Sickett his River," whichwasgranted to said Redding
by the selectmen of the Towne of Cascoe Bay,   18 Feb. 1678.    (York
County Deeds,   3:53.)    Eleanor Redding,  relict of Thomas Redding,
deceased,   late of Cascoe Bay,    for  £404s.  4d. ,  sells  Mary Higginson,
late relict and executrix ofJoshua Atwater,  late of Boston,   deceased,
merchant,      a house and land upon Westgotoggoe  River  in  Cascoe
Bay,     12 Apr.  1680,   and John Redding of Weymouth,   John Taylor
of Boston,      and John  Donell  of Cascoe  Bay,   and Ruth,      his  wife,
surrender all rights to Mary Higginson,  19 Nov.  1680.    ( Ibid.     3:94. )
It  is apparent that the abovesaid John Redding was the son of
Thomas and Eleanor Redding ofCascoe Bay,   Me.       His father married
at Plymouth,    20 July,   1639,   Eleanor Penny.       The Plymouth Colony
Records,    2:   86,   show that Thomas Reddings left his son in care of
GowenWhite of Scituate about the first of June,   1644.    He took the
oath of allegiance at Cascoe,  5 July,  1653,   and died before  10 Mar.
1673-74.             It is supposed that the abovesaid JohnRedding is  identical
with John,     who married at Sandwich,   22 Oct.  1676,    Mary Bassett.
He certainly resided in Weymouth from 1678 to 1680.

gifts of common lands in Weymouth already bestowed upon him at

wife  to  be  executor.           "Finally  I  doe appoint  my beloved brother
Thomas Dyer and my loveing friend Richard Porter my Overseers.  "

568                                         REED
1.  WILLIAM  REED was made a freeman of the Massachusetts
Bay Colony,   18 May,   1653.   The original list of freemen shows that
he was on that day an inhabitant of Weymouth.       (Massachusetts
Bay Colony Records,  4,   Pt.   1,  p.   460.)   Only church members were
then eligible  to be made freemen or voters  in the New England
towns.
There was a William  Reade who was  elected   a  " Townsman"
(selectman) at Weymouth, 26 Nov. 1651.   Theabove-namedWilliam
Reedwas then ineligible and could not have been the manwho was
elected  townsman.          The  following  items  from  Weymouth  Town
Records appear to relate to the above-named William Reed:    " Mary
Read,  daughter of William Read died 16 Apr.  1655."    "John Vining
and Margaret  daughter  of  William  Read were  married,     11  May
1657."   On11 Jan. 1657-58, "William Readpayd Thos.  Dyer2s.  6d.
for  2000 bolts" cut on the Town Common.        On 6 Apr. 1658,     " the
Townsmen ordered that the Widow Read shall have liberty to take
in a garden plott before her House."    On 6 Feb.  1659-60,   " it  was
further granted that WidowAvis Read should have a swamp lott by
virtue that  her  Husband was then an Inhabitant  when the sayd
swamp lotts were granted. "
WidowReadwas granted ten acres in the First Division and thirty
acres  in the Second Division,   14 Dec.  1663.    In a deed from John
Whitman to  John Vining,    dated 19 Dec.  1670,    "the  Land of the
Widdow Avis Reed"  is  mentioned.      (Suffolk Deeds,   11:   183,    184.)
The abovesaid items show that  William  Read (Reed)  was an in-
habitant  of Weymouth from  1653 to  1658,    and that  his wife and
widow lived there from 1653 to  1670.    No settlement of the estate
ofWilliam Reed,  or of his widow Avis,  has been found after diligent
search.
William Reed married at  Long Sutton,  in Somersetshire,   26 Oct.
1635,    Avis Chepman of Knole,  but it must be remembered that no
positive proof has yet been obtained which  shows  that  the  Long
Sutton man and the Weymouth man were one and the same William
Reed,  except the name Avis.
For various reasons the following  are believed to have been the
children ofWilliam and Avis Reed ofWeymouth, born between 1635
and 1658:
Children:
Margaret,        bp.   at Long Sutton,   20 Jan.  1635-36;     m.    at Wey-
mouth,     11  May,   1658,   John Vining of Weymouth;   she d.    6
July,   1659.
Hannah,    m.    2 Dec. 1658,  Nicholas Whitmarsh ofWeymouth.
Mary,    d.    at Weymouth,    unm.    16 Apr. 1655.
2.  William,   resided inWeymouth.
Ruth,    m.   19 Dec. 1662,  John Whitman,   Jr.,   of Weymouth and
d.  the next year.
3.  Thomas,    resided in Weymouth.
John,   b.    near 1649;    removed to Taunton (now Dighton).          He
enlisted from Weymouth as a soldier inKingPhilip's War, 1676.

ZACHARY  RHODES appears as a landowner inWeymouth,   1642
to 1644.    On page 268 of the published Land Grants of Weymouth
his name is  incorrectly printed Zakery Reades for  Roades.          On 6
Mar.  1657,      Zachary Roades deposed,   stating that he was about 54
years of age.             From the Register  (33:   428) we learn that "Jeremiah
Rhodes the Sonne of Zachary Rhodes was borne at Pautuxet the 29
of the 4 month [June]  commonly called June in Anno Dom.     1647."
It appears that Zachary  Rhodes married Joanna Arnold,    widow of
Resolved Waterman and Samuel Winsor,  as her third husband.         She
was born 27 Feb. 1617,   and her third husband lived in Providence
and  Pawtuxet,       R.   I.      (Ibid.         33:   437. )     Malachy  Roads   (son  of
Zachary)   and Mary Carder (daughter of Richard)  were married in
Warwick,      R.  I.,    27 May,     1675.    (Ibid.     37:   275),   and John Roades
(son of Zachariah)  and Wait Waterman (daughter  of Resolved of
Providence) were married at Warwick,  12 Feb.  1684-85.                     ( Ibid. )
Mr. Pope in his Pioneers says he went to Rehoboth in 1643 and was
made a freeman of Plymouth Colony 4June,   1645.

RICHARDS
THOMAS  RICHARDS came probably  in the  ship  Mary and
John,    sailing from Plymouth,   20 Mar. 1630,  and arriving at Nantas-
ket,  30 May,   1630.    (Clapp Genealogy,  3.)    He was made a freeman
of the Massachusetts Bay Colony,  13May, 1640.    (Register,   3:   187.)
Hewas born in England,  near 1590,  anddied atWeymouth,   shortly
before 28 Jan. 1650-51.           He married in England Wealthean Loring,
who survived him,  and died in Boston between 3July and 4 Nov.
1679.    Her will is published in the Richards Genealogy,  1861,    pages
5 and6.    His wife was probably a sister to Thomas Loring ofHull.
Children, born in England:
John,2 b.   near 1615;  settled inDorchester andBoston.
Thomas,   d.   unm.   near 1649.
Mary,    m.    7 Dec. 1641,    Thomas Hinckley, Governor of Plymouth
Colony;  d.  24 June,   1659.
Alice,   m.    Maj.       William  Bradford,  Deputy Governor of Plymouth
Colony;  d.    12 Dec. 1671 .
Anna,   m.    Col. Ephraim Hunt of Weymouth.
James,    b.     as early as 1631;  settled in Boston and Hartford,  Conn.
Benjamin,    settled in Boston.
Joseph,   in school in 1651.
Hannah,   d.    in Boston,   10 Nov. 1651.
Samuel,    probably d.    after  1651 .
1.   WILLIAM  RICHARDS was  settled  at  Weymouth before  1
Sept.  1640.    On that day the General Court appointed Thomas Jen-
ner and Thomas White to settle a difference between William Rich-
ards  and John  Turner.        (Massachusetts  Bay  Colony  Records,     1 :
300.)    He first  appears  at  Plymouth and was there taxed 25 Mar.
1633.    He soon removed to Scituate and was there residing,    6 Jan.
1636-37.             He early had lands granted to him in the westernecke,    25
acres,    which had first been given to John Burslem and William Smith
(Weymouth Land Grants,  274.)    He married,   before  1650,      Grace
Shaw, daughter of Abraham Shaw of Halifax,  Eng.,  and of Dedham.
She was baptized at Halifax,    Yorkshire,    15 Aug.  1621.     (Register,
48: 346.)    She survived  her  husband.        He  made his  will  18 Jan.
1680,      and it  was proved 25 July,   1682.    In it he mentions his wife
Grace,    his sons James,   who was to have the homestead,     William,
Joseph,    and Benjamin,  the youngest.       (Suffolk Probate,  6:   388.)
Children,   born at Weymouth:
2.  John,      b.    near 1650.
3.  Joseph,    b.    near 1653.
4.  William,    b.   near 1656.
5.  James,    b.    2 June,    1658.
Benjamin,    b.     19 May,   1660;   d.  unm.  before 17 May,   1683.    His
brother John was appointed administrator.

RIDER
THOMAS¹ RIDER (Ryder)  came in the  ship  Hercules,     sailing
from Southampton,   16 Apr.  1634.    (Drake's The Founders of New
England,     71.)     He settled first  in Weymouth,  but removed to Bos-
ton.        He was entitled to a lot on the east side of Great Pond next to
Mrs.  Richard's mill,  3 Feb.  1651.     (Weymouth Land Grants,    281.)
Hehad other lands granted to him which apparently reverted to the
town.          He married  Elizabeth  Lane,   daughter  of William  Lane  of
Dorchester.             He died before 23 May,   1655,   leaving  his widow with
five small children.
The Boston records state that the parents were members of the
Church at Weymouth,  andcall them ofWeymouth,  10Aug. 1651,   and
4Dec. 1653.    One child not mentioned may have been born at Wey-
mouth.
Childrenbaptized in Boston:
Elizabeth,       bp.    14 Oct. 1649.
Jacob,   bp.    10 Aug. 1651.
Nathaniel,   bp.    4 Dec. 1653.
Hannah,   b.    7 Mar. 1655.

ROGERS
1.   DEA.    JOHN  ROGERS settled in Weymouth before 1643.    He
is probably the John Rogers who was made a freeman of the Massa-
chusetts  Bay Colony,    17  May,     1637.    He was deacon of the First
Church and a townsman (selectman) in 1645,     1646,   1652,     1654,    1655,
1657 and 1659.    He was elected "town recorder," in 1651.    He died
at Weymouth,  11 Feb. 1660-61 .
He made his will 8 Feb. 1660,   and it was proved 13 Apr.  1661.    Το
his wife Judith he gave the new end of his dwelling house with one-
third of his estate for  life.            To his son John Rogers he gave care of
his  estate.             To his  daughter  Mary Rane and his  son-in-law John
Rane,    his  great lot  of 12 acres and 40s.    and £10.             To his  daughter
Lydia White six acres or £5.          To his daughter Hannah Pratt £5.                 To
his daughter Sarah  £15 after marriage or at  18.    Refers to his  son-
in-law Joseph  White,    his son-in-law John Rane,   and Samuel Pratt,
and to his apprentice William Richards.        Overseers,    Thomas White,
John Holbrook and Thomas Dyer.       Inventory taken 20 Feb.  1660-
61.    (Register,    10:   265,   266.)
Children,   born at Weymouth or in England:
Mary,    b.      near 1636;    m.     24 Nov.  1659,   John Rane.
2.   John,    b.      near 1638;    of age in  1660.

Joseph White.
Sarah,    b.     near 1644;   under 18 on 8 Feb.  1660-61.
2.   ELDER  JOHN2 ROGERS (Dea.    John¹)  was born near  1638;
died at Weymouth,   28 Feb.  1709-10,    aged 71.    He married  (1)   at
Weymouth,      8  Jan.  1662,     Mary Bates,     daughter  of Elder  Edward
and Susannah Bates.       She died before 22 Oct.  1683,  and he married
(2)  Judith      , who survived him.      In his will Elder Edward Bates
styles  him,     " my son John Rogers,"  22 Oct.  1683.    He is  probably

setts  Bay Colony,   4;    Pt.   II,   p.    585.)    He took the oath of allegiance
at  Weymouth,    1678-79.           He was Ruling Elder of the First  Church

ROUSE
NICHOLAS ROUSE came in the Charity or Swan to Wessagussett
in June or July,   1622.   He was one of the "four men which escaped"
to Christopher Levett's plantation at Casco on the coast of Maine
in  1623.    In a letter  from John Winter to Robert Trelawny,   dated
7  Oct.  1640,     Winter gives " the names of som men in England that
did know the River of Casco before your [Trelawny's]   pattent was
granted. "    One was, "Nycholas Rouse of Wembery, which dwelt at
the house at Casko with Thomas Alger 10 yeares past.  "    (Trelawny
Papers,     251.)      Wembury is  a parish  in Devonshire six  miles  from
Plymouth.               Winter  was  uncertain  whether  he  was  living   7 Oct.
1640.
ROWE
HUGH¹ ROWE (Roe)  had land granted to him at Weymouth,
west of John Burrell's,  north of Richard Waling's,   on King Oke Hill,
north of John Whitman's,   south of Robert Lovell's.         (Land Grants,
259,     264,     265,      268,    276.)    He was granted lot 21,   of eight  acres,     in
the First  Division,  14 Dec. 1663,   and lot 51 of twenty-four acres in
the Second Division.         (Ibid.      282,    283.)     His wife was Abigail
and he lived  in  Weymouth from 1655  to  1663  and perhaps  for  a
longer  period.        According  to  Savage's Genealogical  Dictionary  he
removed to  Suffield,    Conn.,    where he died 5 Aug.  1689.    His wife
Abigail died there 3 Sept. 1689.   He had 60 acres granted to him in
Suffield 24 June,    1674.
He must be distinguished from Hugh Rowe of Gloucester,     1667.
Children by wife Abigail:
Esther,       d.     at Weymouth,  11 July,    1655.
Samuel,      b.       at  Weymouth,   14 Jan.  1655-56;    d.     at Suffield,    Conn.  ,
1 Mar. 1688,   unm.
Peter,    called a son in his father's will;    d.   4 Feb. 1739.
Mary,   m.  -  Denslow.
Elizabeth,     m.                                   Merrill  of Saybrook,     Conn.
Abigail,    m.       Thomas Taylor.

SANDERS
JOHN SANDERS was one of the men who came in Thomas Wes-
ton's Company to Wessagusset in July,  1622,  in the Charity or Swan.
He was overseer of the plantation while Weston sailed to Virginia in
the Charity.             He is  the man upon whom Weston was disposed  to
place the blame for the failure ofthe company to withstand the perils
of the winter of 1622-23 when Gorges met him at Plymouth late in
the year  1623.    He was probably one of the trustees of Ferdinando
Gorges Patent in the Province ofMaine,  and gave the control over to
the Massachusetts  Bay Colony at  Wells,   27  May,    1662.     (British
Calendar of State Papers,   1661-68.)     He probably is the man who
was employed by John Winter at  Richmond's Island some time be-
tween the last of July,   1641,  and 10June,   1642.    (Trelawny Papers,
327.)     His name also appears in the accounts which John Winter sent
to Robert Trelawny from Richmond's Island in 1634,   with a letter
dated at Richmond's Island,  18 June,  1634.    (Ibid.     38.)
He,   or another of the same name,   witnessed a will at Wells,    8 Jan.
1654,    and made oath to it 17 July,   1657,  at which time he was styled
Lieut.      John  Sanders.         (York  Deeds,    1:   61,     62.)     He and his  wife
Ann,    for  £150 and other good causes,  sell John Cutts of Portsmouth
"that Mansion house" being neare Cape PorpusRiver in the parish of
Wells "commonlycalled by the name ofJohn Sanders Farme"  with
400 acres,    9 Oct.  1663.    (York Deeds,   1:   143.)
In another deed confirming unto him his land the Indian Flewellen
styled  him  "Senior,"  19 Feb.  1660,   and in another deed,    dated  12
Feb.  1660,   John Bush called him "my father-in-law. "     ( Ibid.      1 :    107.)
It appears that his earliest grant of 150 acres in Wells was made by
Thomas Gorges,    Governor of the Province of Maine,   14 July,    1643,
and that Ezekiel Knight of Wells sold him a dwelling house there 20
Aug. 1645.     (York Deeds,    1,    Pt.    2:    11,    12.)
"Ann Sanders,  executrix of the last will of her lately deceased hus-
bandJohn Sanders Senior of Cape Porpus, with the consent of Thomas
Sanders,   eldest son of the deceased,   sells AndrewAlger of Cape Porpus
 - 621 - 
SHAW                                611
for  £7,    100 acres at Cape Porpus now in possession of Mr.  Francis
Johnson ofBoston," 21 Oct.  1670.     (Ibid.    2:  127.)   " John Sanders,
Sr. ,  witnessed adeedfromJohnBushandGrace, hiswife, both ofCape
Porpus to Thomas Mussell" on 24 Nov. 1669.     ( Ibid.     2 :    131.)
"John Sanders Senior ofCape Porpus,  planter, being verysicke and
weakeinbody, madehis will 13June 1670,  andit wasproved24June,
1670.    To his wife Ann Sanders he gave the use of his house and
lands for life,   and at her decease the same to his son Thomas Sanders,
and at his decease to his son John Sanders.       To his son John Sanders
1,000 acres eight or nine miles above Cape Porpus River Falls.           The
rest of his estate to all of his children,    unnamed.         Widow Sanders
returned the inventory" 23 Aug. 1670.    (Maine Wills,   18,    19.)

SHEPARD
RALPH SHEPARD,  aged 29,   his wife Thankes,  aged 23,  and their
daughter  Sara,   aged 2,   came in the Abigail  in July,   1635.    They
probably  sailed  from  Stepney,    near  London.          (Hotten's  Original
Lists,     97.)     He first  located in Charlestown,   removed to Dedham,
then to Weymouth,  then to Malden and finally  to  Concord.         By
trade he was a tailor.          He is probably the Ralph Shepard who died
at  Malden,    11  Sept.  1693,   aged 90 years,   according  to the record.
He removed to Rehoboth,   but his allotment was there forfeited 24
Oct.  1643.    (For other details see Ralph Shepard,  Puritan,    1893,    by
Ralph Hamilton Shepard.)
Children:
Sarah,   b.    in England,    1633.
Isaac,     b.     at Weymouth,  20 June,   1639.
Tryall,      b.       at  Weymouth,      19  Dec.  1641;     m.     11  Mar.  1660-61,
Walter Powers.
Thomas,   b.    near 1635; lived in Malden and Milton.
Abraham,   resided in Concord.
Thanks,   b.    at Malden,   10 Feb. 1650-51;   m.   Peter Dill of Chelms-
ford.
Jacob,    b.    at Malden,  June,   1653.
John,   b.   perhaps near  1637.
Walter,   b.      一.

SILVESTER
RICHARD  SILVESTER (Sylvester) desired to be made a freeman
of the Massachusetts Bay Colony,  19 Oct. 1630,  and was made a free-
man 1 Apr.  1634.    (Register,   3:   90,   92.)     He was one of the earliest
settlers  of  Weymouth.        He was  disfranchised  and  fined  £2 on  13
Mar. 1638-39,  for joining in an attempt to organize a church at Wey-
mouth which was not  in  accordance  with  the  Massachusetts  Bay
authorities.                 He sold  his  Weymouth property,    23  Sept.   1640,      and
removed to  Marshfield about 1644.
who called herself his  wife in  1651.

THACHER  (THATCHER)
1.   REV.      THOMAS  THACHER,    son  of  Rev.  Peter  and Anne
Thacher,    was born at Milton Clevedon,   Somersetshire,   1 May,    1620;
died in Boston,     15 Oct.  1678.    His father  was rector of the parish
of St.  Edmund's,   Salisbury,    Wilts,   from 1623 to  1641.    He married
(1) ,     11 May,    1643,   Elizabeth  Partridge,   daughter of Rev. Ralph and
Patience  Partridge,    first  minister  of Duxbury.       She died at Wey-
mouth,     2  June,    1664.    He married  (2)  Margaret  (Webb)  Sheaffe,
widowof Jacob Sheaffe of Boston,  and daughter of Henry Webb of
Boston.
He came to Boston in the ship James,   sailing from Southampton
and arriving in Boston,  4 June,    1635.   He studied with Rev. Charles
Chauncey of  Scituate,  who became president of Harvard College.
He was ordained as minister of the First Church (the North Parish)
of Weymouth,   2 Jan. 1644-45,  and remained in charge till 1667.   He
was installed as first  minister of the Third Church (the Old South
Church) of Boston 16 Feb.  1669-70.          The destruction of the church
records  of the North Parish by fire 23 Apr.  1751,   obliterated much
 - 652 - 
642                                        THAYER
evidence relating to the baptisms,  marriages and burials of the early
families of the town.       Weare justified in assuming that Rev. Thomas
Thacher's  family was born in Weymouth,   and doubtless their bap-
tismal records were in the destroyed records of the North Parish.
Children:
2.  Thomas,        eldest son,  b.   near 1645;   settled in Boston.
Ralph,    or Rodolphus,  second son;  settled  in Duxbury and re-
moved to Chilmark,   Martha's Vineyard.
Peter,     youngest son,  b.   at Salem,   18 July,   1651;   graduate at
Harvard  College,      1671;     minister  of  the  First  Church  of
Milton,     1681 to 1727.
Patience,    m.    William Kemp.
Elizabeth,    m.     (1) Nathaniel Davenport who was killed in King
Philip's  War,    19 Dec. 1675;   m.    (2)  1677,   Samuel Davis.
2.   THOMAS  THACHER (Rev. Thomas,      Rev. Peter¹)  was born
probably at Weymouth near 1645;    died in Boston,  2Apr. 1686.   He
married,   near  1670,     Mary Savage,   daughter of Maj.    Thomas and
Faith  (Hutchinson) Savage,  baptized in Boston,  6 June,   1647,   " aged
about 8 days. "    She died in Boston,   22 July,  1730,   leaving all her

Boston merchant.
Children,  born in Boston:

THOMAS
1.   САРТ.        JOHN  THOMAS appears  in  Weymouth as early  as
1701.    He married,   near  1701,    Lydia  Whitman,   daughter  of Dea.
Abiah and Mary (Ford) Whitman of Weymouth.        She was born near
1678 anddied in 1757.    Capt.  John Thomas died at Braintree,   4Oct.
1714.    Abiah Whitman,  in consideration of the faithful services per-
formed for  Capt.    John Thomas,  my son-in-law,  gives  James Hogg
land in the North Purchase of Taunton,   8 Aug. 1704.    On 13 Sept.
1750,    Rev. Samuel Whitman of Farmington,  Conn.,  made his will in
which he stated that Lydia Whitman lived with his father as a maid
manyyears,  and was married to Capt.   Thomas,  who died and left her
awidow with several children.         He gave her or her children that are
living  £16.             It is  stated that Capt.   John Thomas was an English
eras

shipmaster.            (See New England Historical  and Genealogical Regis-
ter,  49:   172-177.)

TITUS
ROBERT  TITUS was early granted lands in Weymouth.          (Wey-
mouth  Land Grants,    274.)     Robert  Titus,     a husbandman,     of  St.
Katherins,      aged 35,   his  wife  Hannah,   aged 31,   and their  children
John,    aged 8,    and Edmond,   aged 5,  imbarqued in the Hopewell for
New England,   3 Apr. 1635.    He had land granted to him in Boston
adjoining  William  Blackstone's,    14 Dec.  1635.    Soon removed  to
Weymouth and later  to  Rehoboth,  and still  later  to Huntington,
L. I.

TORREY
1.   CAPT.       WILLIAM  TORREY came from  Combe St.   Nicholas
county of Somerset,   England,    to Weymouth in  1640.    He was the
son  of Philip  and Alice  Torrey,     born  and baptized  at  Combe St.
Nicholas,     21  Dec.  1608.    He married (1)  at Combe St.  Nicholas,   17
Mar.  1629,      Agnes Combe,  daughter of Joseph  Combe,  baptized  at
CombeSt.  Nicholas,  4Jan. 1608.   She died soon after their marriage.
He married  (2),    near  1630,    Jane  Haviland,   daughter  of  Matthew
Haviland of Bristol,    Eng.        She was buried at Combe St.  Nicholas,
27 Apr.  1639.    He married  a third wife and settled at Weymouth.
He died at Weymouth,  10 June,   1690.
He was captain,   commissioner and deputy from Weymouth to the
General Court from 1642 to  1645,   1679 and 1683.   For many years
hewas clerk of the House of Deputies in the General Court.             (Water's
Gleanings in England,   pp.   498,     549.)

TORREY ANCESTRY  OF  CHIEF JUSTICE  TAFT
WILLIAM  HOWARD TAFT,    chief justice  of the Supreme Court of
the United States,   in his address at Weymouth in June,   1923,     laid
particular  stress  upon his descent from the Torreys of Weymouth.
His line from Capt.  William¹ Torrey comes from the latter's youngest
son,
ANGELL  TORREY,  born at Weymouth,  10 June,  1657;    married,
before 1690,     Hannah  - Angell Torrey removed to Mendon and
later to Bristol,   R. I.    His son was:
WILLIAM  TORREY,  born at Bristol,   R. I.,  17 Dec. 1700;    married
there,   24 Dec. 1724,   Susannah Giddings.     Their son was:
JOSEPH  TORREY,  who married at Mendon,  6 Sept. 1752,    O. S.,
Deborah Holbrook.       They lived in Mendon,  and their son was:
CAPT.     WILLIAM   TORREY,   born  at  Mendon,   23  Nov.  1754;
died there 16 Sept.  1817,   in his 63d year.       He married at Mendon,
20 July,     1788,    Anna  Davenport, daughter of Seth   (Seth,      Samuel,
John,     Thomas¹),  and Chloe (Daniels) Davenport.     She was born at
Mendon,    8 Sept.  1765,   and died there  1 Aug.  1842,   aged seventy-
seven years.          She married (2),   3 Feb.  1822,    Capt.    Peter  Holbrook.
Capt.   William Torrey resided on the old Torrey homestead in Men-
don.        Their son was:
SAMUEL  DAVENPORTS TORREY,   born at  Mendon,    14 Apr.
1789;    died at  Millbury,   23 Dec.  1877.    He was a Boston merchant
andmarried twice.     He married (2),  in 1824,   Susan Holman Waters,
daughter of Asa and Susan (Holman)  Waters.       She was baptized at
Sutton,    11 Dec. 1803,  and died at Millbury in 1866.   Their daughter
was:
LOUISA  MARIA  TORREY, born in Boston,  11 Sept. 1827;    died
in  San Diego,   Cal. ,  21 May,  1891,  aged sixty-four years.      She married
as his second wife,  26 Dec. 1853, JudgeAlphonso Taft of Cincinnati,
Ohio.       Their son was:
WILLIAM  HOWARD TAFT,  born at Cincinnati,   Ohio,   15 Sept.
1857.   He married Helen Herron, daughter of Hon. John W. Herron.
He was the  twenty-sixth  President  of  the  United  States.            Their
children are:

VINING
1.   JOHN  VINING had five acres of land granted to him by the

VINSON  (VINCENT,   VINCETT)
1.   JOHN¹  VINSON came to  Weymouth from  London  (Nash's
Sketches  of  Weymouth,    194)  before 1675.    He was not the son of
William Vinson of Gloucester,   as  his  son John died before  1682.
(Records  of  the  Quarterly  Courts of Essex  County,   8:     295.)    He
took the oath of allegiance at Weymouth in 1678 or  1679,    and died
there 20 Sept.  1718.   He married, before 1675,  Sarah -    whodied
his  widow at  Weymouth,    9 Dec.  1729.    James  Richards  of Wey-
mouth called him his uncle in 1701.
,
Administration on his estate was granted to his sons John Vinson
and Samuel Vinson,  both of Weymouth,  8 Dec. 1718.    The inventory,
calls  the  deceased  a house carpenter.        (Suffolk  Probate,    21 :   199,
200.)
Children,  born at Weymouth:
2.  John,       b.    28 July,   1675 or 1676.
3.  Samuel,    not in order,   of age 8 Dec. 1718.
4.  Ebenezer,    b.   26 Mar. 1684.
Sarah,    probably adaughter,   m.   11 Dec. 1705,
Ruth,    probably adaughter,   m.   23 Apr. 1715,   Abiezer Holbrook
ofWeymouth.
2.   САРТ.     JOHN  VINSON  (John¹)  was born at Weymouth,     28
July,     1675 or 1676;    married,  before 1696,  Sarah Kingman,  daughter
of Thomas and Rebecca Kingman of Weymouth.
John Vinson of Weymouth,  gentleman,  made his will 23 July,   1756,
and it  was proved 5 Nov.  1756.    Therein he mentions his grandson
John Vinson,      his  housekeeper  Elizabeth Smith,    his daughter Ruth,
now deceased,    his  son Thomas Vinson,    his daughter  Sarah  Nash,
and his  son Samuel to be maintained so long as he is  bereft  of his
reason;    his son-in-law Jacob Nash to be executor.     (Suffolk Probate,
51 :   709-711.)     He entered his intention of marriage with  Elizabeth
Smith at Weymouth,  25 July,   1755,   but did not marry her.

WALFORD
THOMAS  WALFORD,   a blacksmith,    came to Wessagusset with
the Gorges Company about the middle of Sept. 1623.    In the com-
pany  were  Rev.   William   Morrell,       William   Blackstone,       Samuel
Maverick,     John  Bursley,     William  Jeffrey  and others.         Morrell  re-
turned to England,   Blackstone removed to Shawmut,   Maverick to
Winnisimmet,    and Walford to Mishawum (Charlestown).           When the
ancient planters first  arrived at Mishawum,   in 1629,   they found one
house erected and occupied by Thomas Walford,  the smith.        Accord-
ing  to  the  town records  of Charlestown,    written in the year  1664,
Thomas Walford,   a smith,    occupied a house that was " thacht and
palisadoed,"  situated  on the southern slope of the hill,  a little  way
up from the side of Charles River.        " For comtempt of authority and
for  confronting  officers, "  Walford  was  fined  forty  shillings  by the
 - 732 - 
722                                         WALTHAM
Massachusetts Bay Company,    20 Oct.  1631.    He paid the fine by
killing a wolf.         His goods were sequestrated for debts,  3 Sept.  1633,
and he removed to Portsmouth,   N. H.,  wherehediedbefore 27 June,
1667.    His wife was Jane     ,who deposed 27 June,  1667,      stating
that she was 69 years of age.       In his will,  made 15 Nov. 1666,    and
proved27June,  1667,  he mentions his grandchildren Thomas Walford
and Jeremiah Walford;  his grandchildren John Westbrook and Mary
Hingson;    his  son-in-law  Thomas  Hingson;    his  grandchild  Mary
Homes and her husband John Homes;   his daughter Peverly and
John Peverly land"before his father's dore; "  his wife Jane Walford;
his grandchildren Martha Walford,   Sarah Jones and Mary Savage;
his daughter Westbrook;  his grandchildren Samuel Jones and Hester
Savage;   his  son-in-law John Westbrook;     his  servant  John Reed.
His executors,   Henry Sherburne and Richard Tucker,  both of Ports-
mouth.          Witnesses:   Richard Sloper and Nicholas Doe.          Jane Wal-
ford,      widow,    aged 69 or  thereabouts,    deposed  that  her  husband
Thomas Walford gave his daughter Elizabeth Savage land lying be-
tweenWilliam Brookins and Mary Hincksons about nine years before
hedied,  27 June, 1667.   John Homes, aged 26 or thereabouts, deposed
to the same on same day;   Mary Brooken,  aged 32 or thereabouts,
confirmed the depositions;      Martha  Westbrook,    aged 22 or  there-
abouts,  confirmed the foregoing.       On 1 Mar. 1680,   Jeremiah Walford
called John Amazeen his father-in-law,  and states that his  brother
Thomas Walford is now deceased.      Mary Musset and Martha More
call themselves grandchildren  of Thomas  Walford,    Sr. ,   deceased,    8
Mar.  1680,    and Jean Goss,  Hannah Jones,   Mary Brookin and Eliza-
beth Savage were heirs  7 Sept.  1681.     (New Hampshire  Probate
Records,     I:  87-92. )
WALTHAM  (WALTON)
HENRY  WALTHAM,   a member of the Fishing Company,   and a
merchant,    was settled at Weymouth as  early as 1635.   He was a
partner in the mill with Thomas Richards,   and brought suit against
Richards for the division of one dwelling house belonging to the mill
inWeymouth,   10 Mar. 1640.    (Lechford's Note-Book,  351.)    Jeremy
Gould of Rhode Island and William Jeffreys  of Weymouth gave a
bond in which Gould agreed to sell him certain lands in Weymouth
before  24 Aug.  1641.    (Ibid.      372.)    He sold  his  house  and land
grantedby the town to Rev. Thomas Thatcher,  minister of the First
Church,  5Aug. 1656.    He died at Weymouth,  29 Jan. 1658-59.             His
wife's  name was Ann
He was a deputyfromWeymouth in 1636.    Hazillpenah Willockes
was dwelling in his house 21 Oct.  1653.    (Register,  5:  303.)
Children:
William,  bur.   3 Nov. 1640,  unm.;  called son of William.
Thomas,    living inWeymouth,   1640.
Henry,   living in Weymouth,    1640.
Anne,  b..
Phillyne,   b.      —.

WEAVER
CLEMENT  WEAVER was early settled at Weymouth,     and had
lands granted to him there.       The General Court  fined  him ten shil-
lings for drunkenness 2 June,   1640,   and Mr. Barnard for giving him
strong water while at work at Barnard's house,  on the same date.
(Massachusetts Bay Colony Records,   1:  297.)    He removed to New-
port,   R. I. ,   as early as 1655.    He is calledSergt.  Clement Weaver,   Sr.
He married  Mary Freeborn and had several children.         On 20 Oct.
1683,    Samuel Hubbard of Newport wrote: "Old Weaver is dead,   near
an hundred years old. "
WEBB
RICHARD¹  WEBB was an early  settler  at  Weymouth and had
about 20 acres granted to him there.       Apparently he purchased his
homestead lot of Rev. Robert Lenthall.          (Weymouth Land Grants,
262.)     He removed to  Boston before  28  Dec.  1644,    when he was
admitted to the First Church of Boston.        His wife  Mary
admitted there 22 Mar. 1645.    He died in Boston,  2July,   1659.    Son
Joseph chose his uncle John Upham to be his guardian.           Esther Pierce
was Richard's daughter-in-law.
Children,    born at Weymouth:

ae.   about 4 yrs.   12 Jan.  1644-45.
Nehemiah,    b.     19 Oct.  1641,   son of Richard;  bp.   at First Church of
Boston,    ae.    about 3 yrs,   12 Jan.  1644-45.

THOMAS WESTON was born about 1585,  possibly in Shropshire,
Eng.;   apprenticed to Rowland Heylin of the London Company of
Ironmongers,   5Aug. 1602;  admitted to the freedom of the Company
of Ironmongers,   21 Mar. 1611;  visited Holland in 1619;  treasurer of
the London Company of merchant adventurers.       He married,   about
1620,       Elizabeth  Weaver,  daughter of Christopher Weaver,   a mer-
chant,   sometime of Stamford in Lincolnshire and sometime of Lon-
don,  and his wifeAlice (Greene) Weaver.       Early in 1622 Weston and
John Beauchamp sent over to New England the little  Sparrow of
thirty tons to fish  and trade.      The master of the Sparrow anchored
at the fishing grounds,  but sent a boat to Plymouth with six or seven
men,   the advance guard of Weston's colony.        In March,   1622,   Weston
fitted out two more ships,  the Charity and the Swan.         While loading
the ships at London,  the purser of the Charity,  one Philemon Powell,
who styled himself a leather-seller  of London,   was arrested and im-
prisoned.            The voyage was thus delayed until April or  May,    1622,
whenthe two ships sailed for New England.        The Sparrow fished at
Monhegan,  came to Plymouthand went onto Virginia.            The Charity
sailed to Wessagusset,   and from there to Plymouth,  and then returned
to  London.             The  Swan  stayed  at  Wessagusset.          Weston  himself
came in 1623 "in the disguise of a blacke-smith."    He sailed many
times between England and America.         He returned to England and
died in Bristol near 1646.    His will was exhibited for probate in the
Provincial  Court of Maryland in 1647.    His wife Elizabeth survived
him.            Their only surviving child,  Elizabeth,  born in 1632,   was brought
to New England in  1639 or 1640,    and lived in the home of Moses
Maverick of  Marblehead.         She married Roger Conant the younger,
and their first  child,   John Conant,  was born in  1650.    She went to
Ireland,   where her husband died 15 June,   1672.    His widow returned
to Salem in 1684,    and died at Marblehead perhaps.         (Proceedings
of Massachusetts Historical Society,   54 pp.     165-172.)

1.   ENSIGN  JOHN  WHITMAN came as early as 1638 and was
made a freeman of Massachusetts Bay Colony,  13 Mar. 1638-39.         He
was chosen one of three "to end small controversies  in Waymoth, "
14 May,   1645,   and on the same day the General Court confirmed him
"ensigne of the company at Waymoth. "     (Massachusetts Bay Colony
Records,    2:    97,   98.)     He was deacon of the First Church and died at
Weymouth,   13 Nov. 1692.     His wife Ruth  -, died at Weymouth,
17 Oct.  1662.

WHITMARSH
1.   JOHN  WHITMARSH,   aged 39,   Alice  Whitmarsh,   his  wife,
aged 35,     their  children James,  aged 11,   Jane,  aged 7,   Onesephorus,
aged 5,   and Richard,   aged 2,   sailed from Weymouth,   Eng. ,   in Rev.
Joseph Hull's Company,  on or near 20 Mar.  1634-35.          He received
grants of land inWeymouth and settled there.     His lands included
"two acres upon the plain,  .....  three acres upon King  Oak Hill,
two acres in the west field" besides other lots.    About 1644 a
description of the lands of Nicholas, Richard,  Onesephorus and Simon
Whitmarsh mentions "nine acres  in the westerneck  first  given  to
their  father  John  Whitmarsh  dec'd. "     In a description  of  John
Harding's  land mention is  made of land "which he gave to John
Whitmarsh sonn of the aforesaid John  Whitmarsh. "    Hence John
Whitmarsh,    Sr.,  died near 1644.

2.  JOHN  WHITMARSH (John¹) was born in England;   married,
near 1654,     Sarah Harding, daughter of John Harding.
Administration on the estate of John Harding, late ofWeymouth,
deceased, wasgrantedtoJohnWhitmarsh inright of his wife,  only child
of said Harding,  31 Oct. 1682.    He was a housewright.      He served
in King Philip's War in Capt.  William Torrey's Company, 1675.
Hemade his will 22 May,  1695,  and it was proved 15 Dec.  1709.
In it  he mentions his eldest  son John,   his son Ebenezer,   his son
Zachariah,    if he returns from sea, his son Ezra,  his daughters Sarah,
Mary,     Deborah,  Judith Shaw and Ruth;   son Ezra Whitmarsh  to
be executor.            Friends  Edward Bates  and Joseph  Dyer,    overseers.
If  son Zachariah should miscarry,  as my son James did,   and not
come home,  his part to be divided betwixt my three grandchildren,
Joseph Petty,  JohnBates and Richard Whitmarsh.      (SuffolkProbate.
17:70.)

JOHN  WOODCOCK,  aged between 20 and 30,  sailed from Wey-
mouth,  Eng. ,   on or near 20 Mar. 1634-35 with Hull's Company.       He
settled in Roxbury and sold his house and land there 6June,   1651.

WILDS
NORFOLK PROBATE RECORDS
WILLIAM WILDS,  by wife Judith,  had Abigail  T.  and James  L.
Wilds,     to whom the father  was guardian,     1  May,    1852.    (20366.)
They inherited from the estate of Israel D. Wilds.
JAMES L.  WILDS died at Weymouth before 29 Apr. 1843,  leaving
six brothers and sisters.        The probate papers also call him James
C. Wilds.              (20367.)
MARIA F.  WILDES,   wife of James L. Wildes, died at Weymouth,
26 Sept. 1873,  leaving her father Robert F. Burrell.         (20368.)
MARY WILDS,      widow,    died at Weymouth before  10 Mar.  1860.
Her next ofkinwereHannah P. Durrell,  Solomon L. Wilds of Boston,
William Wilds,   Mary Lovell, wife ofJames,   Selinia Wilds,   and Susan
Clift,    wife of Moses R. Clift of Marshfield.           (20369.)
SELINA WILDES,  single woman,  died at Weymouth,  16 Mar. 1881.
Heirs:   Mary Lovell,    widow,   Susan Clift  of Marshfield,    widow,    sis-
ters;  Solomon L. Wildes of Boston, brother;  Israel D. Wildes,   James
L. Wildes,      William W. Wildes,  all of Weymouth,   Abby T.  Wildes
and Henry S.  C.  Durrell  (under guardianship of Joseph Titcomb),
both of Kennebunk,   Me.,  children of a deceased brother and sister.
(22341.)
